poli.colombia.conflict-peace.el-no-que-g.title: El No ganó por 53.894 votos
poli.colombia.conflict-peace.el-no-que-g.hook: El 2 de octubre de 2016 el No le ganó al Sí por 53.894 votos, con 37% de participación.
poli.colombia.conflict-peace.el-no-que-g.author: author-humanities-1

reviewed.notes: The vote totals did not differ by the 53.894 the title claims. Replaced with the Registraduria escrutinio: No 6.431.376 (50,21%), Si 6.377.482 (49,78%), margin 53.894.

poli.colombia.conflict-peace.el-no-que-g.body:
El 26 de septiembre de 2016, en Cartagena, el gobierno y las FARC firmaron con bolígrafos hechos de casquillos de bala. Seis días después, el 2 de octubre, el país votó si refrendaba el acuerdo.

Los números del escrutinio de la Registraduría: No, 6.431.376 votos (50,21%); Sí, 6.377.482 (49,78%). Diferencia, 53.894 votos, menos de medio punto porcentual. Participación, 37,43%, o sea que casi dos de cada tres colombianos habilitados no fueron a votar. El acuerdo necesitaba superar un umbral de 13% del censo —4.536.992 votos— y lo superó con holgura; lo que no logró fue ganar.

Nadie lo esperaba: las encuestas daban al Sí por márgenes amplios. Y lo interesante para quien estudia instituciones es lo que vino después. El plebiscito era jurídicamente no vinculante en el sentido de que no derogaba nada por sí mismo, pero políticamente era imposible ignorarlo. El gobierno renegoció con los promotores del No, se firmó un texto nuevo el 24 de noviembre en el Teatro Colón, y esta vez la refrendación la hizo el Congreso, no las urnas.

Un referendo que perdió y aun así cambió el texto que aprobó.

recall.question: ¿Qué pasó con el acuerdo después de que ganó el No?
recall.answer: Se renegoció con los voceros del No, se firmó una versión nueva el 24 de noviembre de 2016 en el Teatro Colón y la refrendación se hizo por el Congreso en lugar de las urnas. El plebiscito no derogaba nada por sí solo, pero cambió el contenido del acuerdo.

sources.title: Plebiscito sobre los acuerdos de paz de Colombia de 2016

poli.colombia.political-system.la-paz-qu.title: La paz que consistió en repartirse el poder
poli.colombia.political-system.la-paz-qu.hook: Liberales y conservadores acordaron turnarse la presidencia durante dieciséis años. Funcionó, y ese fue el problema.
poli.colombia.political-system.la-paz-qu.author: author-humanities-1

reviewed.notes: The 1957 plebiscite approved paridad, not alternacion; alternacion came from the 1958-59 constitutional reform. Diagram accents fixed.

poli.colombia.political-system.la-paz-qu.body:
El 1 de diciembre de 1957 Colombia votó un plebiscito con un resultado que hoy parece imposible: 4.169.294 síes contra 206.654 noes. Fue, además, la primera votación nacional en la que participaron las mujeres. Lo que aprobaron fue la paridad: los ministerios, las gobernaciones y las curules se repartían mitad y mitad entre los dos partidos que se venían matando, sin importar quién ganara.

La otra mitad del pacto, la alternación, no venía en el plebiscito; la agregó enseguida una reforma constitucional tramitada en 1958 y 1959. La presidencia se turnaba cada cuatro años, liberal, conservador, liberal, conservador, de 1958 a 1974. Era una democracia con el resultado escrito por adelantado.

Y funcionó para lo que se diseñó: la violencia partidista entre liberales y conservadores se desplomó. El costo fue que la competencia política dejó de existir. Cualquier fuerza que no fuera liberal o conservadora quedaba fuera del reparto por definición, y los años del Frente Nacional son exactamente los años en que nacen las FARC, el ELN, el EPL y después el M-19.

Un acuerdo de paz que cerró una guerra construyendo la puerta por donde entró la siguiente.

recall.question: ¿Cuál fue el costo institucional del Frente Nacional?

options.text: Debilitó a los dos partidos tradicionales
options.why: al contrario, les garantizó el poder durante dieciséis años.

options.text: Cerró la competencia política
options.why: quien no fuera liberal o conservador quedaba excluido del reparto por diseño, y de ahí salieron las guerrillas.

options.text: Impidió que las mujeres votaran
options.why: el plebiscito de 1957 fue justamente la primera votación nacional con voto femenino.

poli.democracy.arrow.no-voting-rule-can-.title: Arrow proved the repair shop is empty
poli.democracy.arrow.no-voting-rule-can-.hook: Condorcet found one broken rule. Arrow proved that the repair shop is empty.

series.title: Why democracy is hard to define

poli.democracy.arrow.no-voting-rule-can-.author: author-humanities-1

reviewed.notes: Episode had no curiosity gap into episode 4; added one on giving up a condition.

poli.democracy.arrow.no-voting-rule-can-.body:
The natural reaction to Condorcet's cycle is engineering: majority rule is a crude device, so build a better one. Borda counts, runoffs, approval, whatever it takes. Kenneth Arrow, writing a doctoral thesis at Columbia, asked the question properly. Instead of testing rules one at a time, he wrote down the handful of things *any* acceptable rule should do, and asked whether anything satisfies them all.

Four conditions. Accept every possible set of individual rankings. If everyone prefers x to y, rank x above y. Decide x against y using only how people rank x against y. And do not let one person's ranking dictate the outcome no matter what anyone else says.

Nothing does all four. Not a single rule, not now, not ever, once there are at least three alternatives. The result appeared in *Social Choice and Individual Values* in 1951, and it won him the Nobel in 1972.

The third condition is the one doing the damage.
poli.democracy.arrow.no-voting-rule-can-.rigor:
Let $X$ be a set of alternatives with $|X| \ge 3$ and $N = \{1,\dots,n\}$ a finite set of individuals. A **social welfare function** $f$ maps each profile $(\succsim_1,\dots,\succsim_n)$ of complete transitive orders on $X$ to a complete transitive order $\succsim_S$ on $X$.

**Arrow's theorem (1951).** No $f$ satisfies all of:

- **Unrestricted domain.** $f$ is defined on every profile of complete transitive orders.
- **Weak Pareto.** If everyone strictly prefers $x$ to $y$, then $x \succ_S y$.
- **Independence of irrelevant alternatives.** $\succsim_S$ restricted to $\{x,y\}$ depends only on each $\succsim_i$ restricted to $\{x,y\}$.
- **Non-dictatorship.** There is no $i$ such that $x \succ_i y \Rightarrow x \succ_S y$ for all profiles and all $x,y$.

Two readings of the fine print. The transitivity of $\succsim_S$ is an assumption, not a conclusion — it is exactly the property Condorcet's cycle destroyed. And IIA is what forbids the rule from using *strength* of preference: a Borda count violates it, which is why inserting a hopeless candidate can flip a Borda winner.

Arrow's own 1951 statement used monotonicity and non-imposition; the second edition of 1963 replaced them with the Pareto condition above, which is how the theorem is now taught.

Four conditions, no rule. Which leaves exactly one move, and every working democracy has already made it: decide which condition you are willing to lose.

recall.question: Which Arrow condition does the Borda count violate?

options.text: Independence of irrelevant alternatives
options.why: Borda scores depend on where the other candidates sit, so adding a no-hoper can flip the winner.

options.text: Weak Pareto
options.why: a unanimously top-ranked alternative always wins a Borda count.

options.text: Unrestricted domain
options.why: the Borda count accepts any profile of rankings you hand it.

options.text: Non-dictatorship
options.why: no single Borda voter can override the rest.

sources.title: A Difficulty in the Concept of Social Welfare
sources.author: Kenneth J. Arrow

poli.democracy.arrow.the-second-impossib.title: Remember social choice? There is a second impossibility
poli.democracy.arrow.the-second-impossib.hook: Arrow killed the perfect voting rule. Gibbard and Satterthwaite killed the honest one.
poli.democracy.arrow.the-second-impossib.author: author-humanities-1
poli.democracy.arrow.the-second-impossib.body:
When you met social choice as an aggregation problem, the target was a rule turning individual preferences into a group ranking, and Arrow's theorem said no rule is at once universal, Pareto-respecting, independent and non-dictatorial. That was a statement about the *output*.

There is a twin result about the *input*. Even if you accept a flawed rule, you would still like voters to have no reason to lie to it. Allan Gibbard in 1973 and Mark Satterthwaite in 1975 proved you cannot have that either: any deterministic rule that can elect at least three different candidates, and is not a dictatorship, has situations where some voter does strictly better by submitting a ranking they do not hold.

So strategic voting is not a defect of bad rules or dishonest citizens. It is a theorem, and every electoral reform argument you will ever read is really an argument about which manipulations to tolerate.
poli.democracy.arrow.the-second-impossib.rigor:
Let $|X| \ge 3$ and let $f$ map profiles of strict orders to a single winner in $X$.

- $f$ is **onto** if every $x \in X$ wins for some profile.
- $f$ is **strategyproof** if no voter $i$ ever strictly prefers the outcome of a false report to the outcome of their true one, holding the other reports fixed.
- $f$ is **dictatorial** if some fixed $i$ always gets their top choice.

**Gibbard–Satterthwaite (1973, 1975).** If $f$ is onto and strategyproof, then $f$ is dictatorial.

The link to Arrow is a construction, not an analogy. From a strategyproof $f$ one builds a social welfare function satisfying unrestricted domain, weak Pareto and independence of irrelevant alternatives; Arrow then forces a dictator, and that dictator pulls back to $f$. Independence and strategyproofness are two faces of the same demand: nothing outside the pair $\{x,y\}$ — neither an irrelevant alternative nor a lie about one — may change how the rule ranks $x$ against $y$.

The escape hatches are where the subject becomes constructive: randomise the rule, restrict the domain to single-peaked preferences, where median rules are strategyproof, or allow transfers, which is where mechanism design starts.

recall.question: What exactly does the Gibbard–Satterthwaite theorem rule out?

options.text: Any voting rule producing a transitive group ranking
options.why: that is Arrow's theorem, about aggregation rather than manipulation.

options.text: A non-dictatorial deterministic rule with three or more possible winners in which honest voting is always safe
options.why: some profile always rewards a lie.

options.text: Voting rules that look past first preferences
options.why: ranked rules are allowed; they are simply manipulable like everything else.

sources.title: Manipulation of Voting Schemes: A General Result
sources.author: Allan Gibbard

poli.democracy.condorcet-paradoxes.the-m.title: The majority can want A over B, B over C, and C over A
poli.democracy.condorcet-paradoxes.the-m.hook: Three voters, three options, and the majority prefers A to B, B to C, and C to A.

series.title: Why democracy is hard to define

poli.democracy.condorcet-paradoxes.the-m.author: author-humanities-1

reviewed.notes: Episode pointed forward to episode 4 and skipped episode 3; gap rewritten to hand off to the repair attempt.

poli.democracy.condorcet-paradoxes.the-m.body:
Ana ranks A, B, C. Beto ranks B, C, A. Caro ranks C, A, B. Now vote on pairs. A beats B two to one. B beats C two to one. And C beats A two to one.

Nobody was irrational. Every voter has a perfectly ordinary, transitive ranking. The cycle appears only when you add them up: majority rule takes three sensible orders and returns a loop. Which means "what the majority wants" can simply fail to exist, and whoever controls the order of the votes controls the outcome. Put your favourite last and it wins, because it only has to survive one round.

The Marquis de Condorcet found this in 1785, in an essay mostly about whether juries get verdicts right. He died in a revolutionary prison in 1794 and the paradox was more or less forgotten until the 1940s.

Here is what the cycle looks like written out.
poli.democracy.condorcet-paradoxes.the-m.rigor:
Write $x \succ_M y$ for "a strict majority ranks $x$ above $y$". In the profile above,
$$A \succ_M B, \quad B \succ_M C, \quad C \succ_M A,$$
so $\succ_M$ is complete but not transitive, even though each $\succ_i$ is a complete transitive order.

A **Condorcet winner** is an alternative that beats every other in a pairwise majority vote. This profile has none. That is the content of the paradox: the "beats" relation induced by majority rule need not have a maximal element.

How common is it? Under the *impartial culture* assumption — each voter independently draws one of the $3! = 6$ strict orders uniformly — the probability that three alternatives produce a cycle rises with the electorate and tends to about $8.77\%$. Impartial culture is a deliberately pessimistic model: real electorates cluster, and clustering is exactly what kills cycles — which episode 4 will cash in. The first instinct, though, is to blame the instrument: majority rule is crude, so build a better rule. Episode 3 is about why nobody can.

recall.question: In a Condorcet cycle, who is behaving irrationally?

options.text: The voters, since their rankings contradict each other
options.why: each voter's own ranking is perfectly transitive.

options.text: Nobody
options.why: the intransitivity is created by the aggregation rule, not by any individual.

options.text: The agenda-setter, who breaks the tie arbitrarily
options.why: the agenda-setter is exploiting the cycle, not causing it.

sources.title: Essai sur l'application de l'analyse à la probabilité des décisions rendues à la pluralité des voix

poli.democracy.deliberation.what-arrow-d.title: An impossibility theorem is a list of things you can give up
poli.democracy.deliberation.what-arrow-d.hook: Arrow's theorem has four hypotheses. Democracies survive by breaking one of them on purpose.

series.title: Why democracy is hard to define

poli.democracy.deliberation.what-arrow-d.author: author-humanities-1
poli.democracy.deliberation.what-arrow-d.body:
Arrow did not prove democracy impossible. He proved four properties are jointly unsatisfiable, and a theorem like that is really a menu.

Give up unrestricted domain and the trouble often evaporates. If preferences are *single-peaked* — each person has a favourite point and likes things less the further you move from it — Duncan Black showed in 1948 that the median voter's ideal point beats everything else pairwise. No cycle. That is why left-right politics is usually stable and three-cornered arguments are not.

Give up ordinal rankings, which is Amartya Sen's line: Arrow's rules may only know who ranks what above what. Let a rule use intensities and the impossibility softens into a design problem.

Give up fixed preferences. Fishkin, List, Luskin and McLean measured real deliberative polls in 2013 and found people's preferences moved measurably closer to single-peaked after discussion. Deliberation does not aggregate preferences; it reshapes them.

Which is how the German Democratic Republic could keep the word. Democracy was never one mechanism. It is a family of answers to "who decides, and how would we know", and Arrow proved the family will never contain a perfect member.

recall.question: Single-peaked preferences rescue majority rule by violating which of Arrow's conditions?

options.text: Unrestricted domain
options.why: single-peakedness excludes some profiles, which is precisely the domain restriction Arrow ruled out.

options.text: Weak Pareto
options.why: unanimity is still respected under single-peaked preferences.

options.text: Non-dictatorship
options.why: the median voter is decisive by position, not by identity, and who is median changes with the issue.

sources.title: Deliberation, Single-Peakedness, and the Possibility of Meaningful Democracy: Evidence from Deliberative Polls
sources.author: Fishkin, List, Luskin and McLean

poli.democracy.electoral-systems.same-ba.title: Same ballots, three rules, three winners
poli.democracy.electoral-systems.same-ba.hook: Twenty-one voters, three candidates, one set of ballots. Three different rules, three different winners.
poli.democracy.electoral-systems.same-ba.author: author-humanities-1
poli.democracy.electoral-systems.same-ba.body:
Twenty-one voters hand in these rankings, and nobody is lying:

- 8 of them rank A first, then B, then C
- 7 of them rank C first, then B, then A
- 6 of them rank B first, then C, then A

Before you read on, pick your winner. Then work out three answers. Who wins under plurality, counting only first preferences? Who wins a two-round runoff between the top two? And who beats *both* rivals in a head-to-head majority vote?

No ballot changes. No voter lies. Only the rule changes. Whichever answer you like best, notice what you just did: you chose a winner by choosing a procedure. Committees, primaries and constitutions make that choice for you, usually without mentioning it.

recall.question: Under plurality, under a runoff, and under head-to-head majority, who wins?
recall.answer: Plurality: A, with 8 first preferences against C's 7 and B's 6. Runoff: A and C advance, B's six voters prefer C, so C wins 13 to 8. Head-to-head: B beats A 13 to 8 and beats C 14 to 7, so B is the Condorcet winner — and B wins under neither of the other two rules.

poli.democracy.electoral-systems.the-was.title: The rule that manufactures two parties
poli.democracy.electoral-systems.the-was.hook: The clearest near-law in political science: count votes this way and you get two parties, whatever the voters wanted.
poli.democracy.electoral-systems.the-was.author: author-humanities-1
poli.democracy.electoral-systems.the-was.body:
Maurice Duverger noticed in 1951 something close to a law of nature: countries that elect one representative per district, by simple plurality, end up with two big parties. Countries with proportional representation end up with many. The electorate's opinions are not the variable. The counting rule is.

Two separate mechanisms do it. The **mechanical** one is arithmetic: a party with 15% spread evenly across every district wins 15% of the votes and zero seats, because it comes second or third everywhere. The **psychological** one is voters reacting to that arithmetic: once you know your favourite cannot win the seat, voting for them feels like throwing the vote away, so you vote for the least-bad survivor. The first effect punishes small parties; the second makes voters do the punishing in advance.

The caveats matter. Canada, India and the United Kingdom all run plurality elections and all have more than two parties, because a party concentrated in one region wins seats there on few national votes. William Riker, reviewing the evidence in 1982, argued the law survives as a tendency, and that the regional exceptions are the tell.

recall.question: Why does plurality voting punish a party with 15% support spread evenly over every district?

options.text: It finishes second or third everywhere, so it wins almost no seats despite winning votes everywhere
options.why: seats go only to district winners.

options.text: Its voters are less likely to turn out
options.why: turnout is not what the mechanical effect describes.

options.text: Proportional formulas round small parties down
options.why: that is a feature of some PR thresholds, not of plurality districts.

sources.title: Political Parties: Their Organization and Activity in the Modern State
sources.author: Maurice Duverger

sources.title: The Two-party System and Duverger's Law: An Essay on the History of Political Science
sources.author: William H. Riker

poli.democracy.median-voter.both-candida.title: Why both candidates walk to the middle
poli.democracy.median-voter.both-candida.hook: Two ice-cream carts on a beach end up side by side in the middle. So do two parties.
poli.democracy.median-voter.both-candida.author: author-humanities-1

reviewed.notes: Diagram text referred to 'voter 3' but the median dot was labelled only 'median voter'; relabelled.

poli.democracy.median-voter.both-candida.body:
Put two ice-cream carts on a straight beach where sunbathers are spread out and always walk to the nearer cart. Wherever your rival parks, you gain by sliding a step toward them. Harold Hotelling wrote that down in 1929 for shops on a road. The carts end up back to back in the middle, which is terrible for the people at the ends and unbeatable for each cart.

Duncan Black in 1948 and Anthony Downs in 1957 saw that elections are the same beach. Line up voters by how much spending they want, let each vote for whichever platform sits closer to their own ideal, and the platform that beats every other head-to-head is the one the *median* voter wants. Not the mean. The median, which is why a rich minority's extreme position moves nothing.

This is the most-used model in political science, and it explains a real annoyance: why parties that fight bitterly end up proposing nearly the same budget. It also fails loudly — with three candidates, with abstention, with primaries, and above all with more than one issue.

Here is the theorem, and the exact place it breaks.
poli.democracy.median-voter.both-candida.rigor:
Let voters $1,\dots,n$ ($n$ odd) have ideal points $x_i \in \mathbb{R}$ and **single-peaked** preferences: each $u_i$ is strictly increasing to the left of $x_i$ and strictly decreasing to the right.

**Black's theorem (1948).** The median ideal point $x_m$ is a Condorcet winner: for any $y \neq x_m$, a strict majority prefers $x_m$ to $y$.

*Why.* Take $y > x_m$. Every voter with $x_i \le x_m$ is strictly closer to $x_m$ than to $y$, and by single-peakedness ranks $x_m$ higher. That is at least $(n+1)/2$ voters, a majority. Symmetrically for $y < x_m$. The "walk toward your rival" story is this argument run as a best response: any platform other than $x_m$ is beaten, so $(x_m, x_m)$ is the unique Nash equilibrium of the two-candidate game.

Now add a second dimension — say spending *and* an unrelated social question. Ideal points sit in $\mathbb{R}^2$, and a median in every direction almost never exists. The McKelvey–Schofield chaos theorem says that when it does not, majority rule can be steered from any point to any other point by a clever sequence of pairwise votes. One dimension: an equilibrium. Two: the agenda-setter owns you.

recall.question: Which assumption is doing the real work in the median voter theorem?

options.text: That voters are selfish
options.why: self-interest is not needed; any single-peaked preference works.

options.text: That preferences are single-peaked along a single dimension
options.why: with two dimensions a Condorcet winner usually fails to exist.

options.text: That turnout is complete
options.why: the theorem runs on whoever votes, though who is median then changes.

options.text: That there are exactly two candidates
options.why: two candidates make the convergence story vivid, but the Condorcet result holds regardless.

sources.title: On the Rationale of Group Decision-making
sources.author: Duncan Black

poli.democracy.theories.almost-every-gov.title: Almost every government on earth calls itself a democracy
poli.democracy.theories.almost-every-gov.hook: The German Democratic Republic built a wall to keep its citizens in, and kept the word in its name.

series.title: Why democracy is hard to define

poli.democracy.theories.almost-every-gov.author: author-humanities-1

reviewed.notes: Recall duplicated the Athens fact card, and one distractor ('Athens spent heavily on jury pay') is true. Replaced with an item on Gallie's contested concept; cards cross-linked.

poli.democracy.theories.almost-every-gov.body:
The German Democratic Republic built a wall to stop its own citizens leaving. The Democratic People's Republic of Korea is a hereditary monarchy with missiles. Neither dropped the word, and neither thought that was funny.

That is not only cynicism, it is a clue. W. B. Gallie in 1956 called this kind of word an *essentially contested concept*: everyone wants it, so everyone defines it in a way they already satisfy. And the disagreement is not new. Athens filled most public offices by lot and treated elections as an aristocratic trick, on the grounds that a lottery cannot be bought. Robert Dahl, in 1971, thought no real state reaches the ideal at all, and coined *polyarchy* for what states actually manage: contested elections, plural sources of information, freedom to organise. Same word, opposite institutions.

So strip it back to the part nobody disputes. Whatever else democracy is, the majority decides. Hold that thought for one episode, because it is about to come apart in your hands.

recall.question: What is Gallie getting at by calling democracy an "essentially contested concept"?

options.text: Nobody can agree on the facts about how democracies behave
options.why: the quarrel is over what the word picks out, not over measurements.

options.text: The word is prized enough that each side builds a definition it already satisfies
options.why: so the argument is endless by construction, not by carelessness.

options.text: The word means nothing at all
options.why: Gallie claims the opposite: it has several defensible meanings, each with a real argument behind it.

poli.institutions.constitutions.la-papel.title: La papeleta que nadie autorizó
poli.institutions.constitutions.la-papel.hook: En 1990 unos estudiantes metieron en las urnas una papeleta que ninguna ley contemplaba. Dos años después el país tenía otra constitución.
poli.institutions.constitutions.la-papel.author: author-humanities-1
poli.institutions.constitutions.la-papel.body:
En marzo de 1990 los colombianos votaban seis papeletas: Senado, Cámara, asamblea, concejo, alcaldía, consulta liberal. Un movimiento estudiantil imprimió una séptima por su cuenta, sin respaldo legal, pidiendo una asamblea constituyente. Nadie estaba obligado a contarla. Aparecieron cerca de dos millones.

El contexto era el peor imaginable: Luis Carlos Galán había sido asesinado en agosto de 1989, y Bernardo Jaramillo y Carlos Pizarro caerían en los meses siguientes. El gobierno recogió el hecho consumado con el decreto 927 de 1990 y autorizó contar la pregunta en las presidenciales del 27 de mayo. La Corte Suprema avaló el decreto. La asamblea se eligió en diciembre y se instaló el 5 de febrero de 1991, con setenta delegatarios y una presidencia repartida entre tres: Álvaro Gómez Hurtado, Antonio Navarro Wolff y Horacio Serpa. Un conservador, un exguerrillero del M-19 y un liberal firmando el mismo texto.

El 4 de julio de 1991 se promulgó la nueva constitución, que reemplazó la de 1886, definió a Colombia como estado social de derecho y creó la tutela, la Corte Constitucional y la Defensoría del Pueblo. Empezó como un papel fotocopiado.

recall.question: ¿Por qué fue jurídicamente rara la séptima papeleta?
recall.answer: Porque no estaba prevista en ninguna norma: fue una iniciativa estudiantil que los jurados contaron de hecho. Solo después el decreto 927 de 1990 legalizó la consulta para las presidenciales de mayo, y la Corte Suprema lo avaló.

poli.institutions.courts.una-hoja-de-pap.title: Una hoja de papel contra el Estado
poli.institutions.courts.una-hoja-de-pap.hook: Sin abogado, en una hoja escrita a mano, y el juez tiene diez días para responder. Así funciona la tutela.
poli.institutions.courts.una-hoja-de-pap.author: author-humanities-1

reviewed.notes: 1.150 'familias' changed to 'nucleos familiares', the Corte's own count in T-025/2004.

poli.institutions.courts.una-hoja-de-pap.body:
El artículo 86 de la Constitución de 1991 hizo algo poco común: le dio a cualquier persona el derecho a reclamar sus derechos fundamentales ante cualquier juez, sin abogado, sin formato y sin costo, y le puso al juez un plazo de diez días. Eso es la acción de tutela.

El efecto no fue solo procesal. La Corte Constitucional escoge cada mes unas pocas tutelas para revisarlas, y esas sentencias —las que empiezan por T— se volvieron el motor de la jurisprudencia de derechos en Colombia. Un mecanismo diseñado para casos individuales terminó fijando política pública.

El ejemplo más grande es la sentencia T-025 de 2004. La Corte acumuló 108 tutelas presentadas por 1.150 núcleos familiares desplazados por el conflicto, y en lugar de resolverlas una por una declaró un «estado de cosas inconstitucional»: no era un juez fallando mal en un caso, era el Estado incumpliendo de forma estructural. La Corte se quedó vigilando el cumplimiento durante años, con autos de seguimiento que siguen saliendo.

La crítica obvia también es seria: nueve magistrados decidiendo cómo se gasta el presupuesto no fueron elegidos por nadie.

recall.question: ¿Qué hizo distinta a la sentencia T-025 de 2004 frente a una tutela corriente?

options.text: Ordenó indemnizar a las 1.150 familias que la presentaron
options.why: la Corte no resolvió el caso con plata para los demandantes.

options.text: Declaró un estado de cosas inconstitucional
options.why: es decir, una falla estructural del Estado y no un error en un caso, con seguimiento de la Corte durante años.

options.text: Fue la primera tutela admitida en Colombia
options.why: la tutela existía desde 1991 y ya se contaban millones.

poli.institutions.presidentialism.two-pe.title: Two branches, both elected, no referee
poli.institutions.presidentialism.two-pe.hook: Linz's argument against presidentialism in one line: two elected branches, both claiming the people, and no referee.
poli.institutions.presidentialism.two-pe.author: author-humanities-1

reviewed.notes: Opened on the publication rather than the claim; first sentence rewritten to lead with the dual-mandate problem.

poli.institutions.presidentialism.two-pe.body:
Two offices, one claim: *the people chose me*. Juan Linz built a short, alarming argument on that in the first issue of the *Journal of Democracy*, 1990: presidential systems carry a structural fault that parliamentary ones do not.

Start with dual legitimacy. The president was elected by the whole country; so was the congress. When they disagree, both can truthfully say the people chose them, and the constitution offers no democratic tiebreaker. In a parliamentary system the question cannot arise, because the executive exists only while it keeps a majority.

Then add rigidity. A fixed term is a promise that a failed president stays for four more years and a successful one leaves anyway. Parliaments can replace a prime minister on a Tuesday afternoon. Linz's third point is the winner-take-all logic: one indivisible prize makes elections zero-sum, which rewards outsiders who campaign against the whole political class.

Scott Mainwaring and Matthew Shugart answer that Linz generalised from Latin America's coups and ignored how much depended on party systems. The United States has run a presidential system for two centuries. Deadlock, though, is not a bug anyone has fixed.

recall.question: What does Linz mean by the "dual legitimacy" problem in presidential systems?

options.text: Presidents are elected twice, in a first round and a runoff
options.why: a two-round election is one mandate, not two.

options.text: Both branches hold a direct popular mandate
options.why: so when they clash, the constitution offers no democratic arbiter.

options.text: Voters split their tickets between parties
options.why: ticket-splitting is a symptom people cite, not the structural claim.

poli.political-economy.collective-action.title: Why the group with more members usually loses
poli.political-economy.collective-action.hook: Sugar producers are few and organised; sugar consumers are millions and silent. Olson explained why that is the normal case.
poli.political-economy.collective-action.author: author-humanities-1

reviewed.notes: Olson's typology is three-way (privileged/intermediate/latent). Ostrom principles 4 and 7 restated correctly, and inshore fisheries are her failure cases - replaced with the Philippine zanjeras.

poli.political-economy.collective-action.body:
A tariff on sugar costs each consumer a few dollars a year and hands each of a dozen producers millions. Consumers outnumber producers a hundred thousand to one and lose every time. Mancur Olson's 1965 book says that is not a scandal, it is arithmetic.

If a benefit reaches everyone in a group whether or not they helped, each member asks a private question: does my share of the gain exceed my cost of acting? In a small group one member's share can be big enough that they act alone and let the rest ride free. In a huge group nobody's share is worth the effort, so the group stays *latent* — a real shared interest with no organisation behind it. Olson's fix is the selective incentive: a private benefit only for participants. Unions offer legal insurance. Professional bodies sell the licence.

Then Elinor Ostrom spent decades finding groups that manage shared resources anyway — Swiss alpine pastures, Spanish irrigation huertas, Japanese common forests, Philippine zanjera canals — some running for centuries. *Governing the Commons* (1990) pulled eight design principles out of the survivors, and she won the Nobel in 2009.
poli.political-economy.collective-action.rigor:
Take a pure public good and a group of $n$ identical members. Each unit provided costs $c$ and yields gross group benefit $V$, shared equally, so each member gets $V/n$ per unit.

- **Efficient** provision requires $V > c$.
- **Individually rational** provision requires $V/n > c$.

The wedge is the factor $n$. As $n$ grows the second condition fails long before the first. That is Olson's claim that large groups are less able to act on a common interest, made precise — with the sharper point that inequality helps: if one member's share $F_i V$ alone exceeds $c$, that member supplies the good and everyone else free-rides. Olson calls such a group *privileged*; between it and the latent group he puts the *intermediate* case, small enough that one member's abstention gets noticed.

Ostrom's reply is that the one-shot payoff table is the wrong model. Her cases are repeated games among people who observe each other, talk, and punish cheaply. Her principles read like conditions for sustaining a cooperative equilibrium with real institutions: clear boundaries, rules fitted to local conditions, users writing their own rules, monitors who *are* the users or answer to them, graduated sanctions, cheap conflict resolution, the right to organise left unchallenged from outside, and, for a commons sitting inside a larger system, nested layers. Monitoring by the appropriators is the cheap part, and cheapness is why it lasts.

recall.question: In Olson's framework, why can a small group often supply a public good that a large group cannot?

options.text: Small groups care more about the outcome
options.why: the total benefit can be identical; what changes is each member's share of it.

options.text: Each member's share of the benefit can cover their own cost of acting
options.why: so someone supplies it and the others free-ride.

options.text: Small groups face lower communication costs
options.why: real, and Ostrom stresses it, but it is not the mechanism Olson's argument turns on.

sources.title: The Logic of Collective Action: Public Goods and the Theory of Groups
sources.author: Mancur Olson

sources.title: Governing the Commons: The Evolution of Institutions for Collective Action
sources.author: Elinor Ostrom

poli.political-economy.institutions-grow.title: Two towns, one fence, three times the income
poli.political-economy.institutions-grow.hook: Same desert, same families, same food, and one side of the fence earns several times the other.
poli.political-economy.institutions-grow.author: author-humanities-1

reviewed.notes: Easterly reviewed the book warmly; his objection is ex-post rationalising and reliance on anecdote, not cherry-picked cases. Corrected.

poli.political-economy.institutions-grow.body:
Nogales, Arizona and Nogales, Sonora are one town cut by a border. Same desert, same families, same food, and by the book's own figures median household income on the north side is roughly three times that on the south. Geography cannot explain it. Culture cannot explain it. Daron Acemoglu and James Robinson, in *Why Nations Fail* (2012), say institutions can, and that the difference is the fence.

Their distinction: **inclusive** institutions secure property broadly, let outsiders into markets and permit creative destruction; **extractive** institutions funnel the surplus to whoever holds power, and so must block the innovation that would displace them. Each kind reproduces itself, which is why poor countries stay poor for centuries instead of converging. Acemoglu, Simon Johnson and Robinson won the Nobel in 2024.

Now the honest part. Jared Diamond and Jeffrey Sachs argue geography does more work than the book allows. Arvind Subramanian points at China: extractive politics, forty years of growth. William Easterly, reviewing it warmly, still objects to the ex-post rationalising and the weight put on anecdote. And the natural experiment underneath the theory has been attacked directly.
poli.political-economy.institutions-grow.rigor:
The empirical core is Acemoglu, Johnson and Robinson (2001), an instrumental-variables argument. Institutions and income are jointly determined, so a regression of GDP on property rights says nothing about causation. Their instrument is the mortality rate of European settlers in a colony centuries ago:

$$\text{settler mortality} \;\rightarrow\; \text{early institutions} \;\rightarrow\; \text{institutions today} \;\rightarrow\; \log(\text{GDP per capita}).$$

The story: where Europeans could survive they settled and built institutions to protect themselves; where they died they built extraction machines, and those persisted. The exclusion restriction is load-bearing — mortality two centuries ago must reach income today *only* through institutions.

David Albouy's 2012 comment, in the same journal, went at the data rather than the logic. Of 64 countries, 36 are assigned mortality rates borrowed from other countries; the underlying figures mix labourers, bishops and soldiers on campaign, whose death rates are not comparable. Correct for that, he argues, and the first stage stops being robust while the IV confidence intervals blow up.

This is what a contested empirical claim looks like from inside. The theory may well be right. The cleanest evidence for it is not clean.

recall.question: What does the settler-mortality instrument need in order to be valid?

options.text: That settler mortality is uncorrelated with institutions
options.why: the opposite: an instrument is useless unless it predicts them strongly.

options.text: That old settler mortality reaches income today only through institutions
options.why: no other channel, such as today's disease burden.

options.text: That institutions are measured without error
options.why: measurement error matters, but it is not the exclusion restriction.

sources.title: Why Nations Fail
sources.author: Daron Acemoglu and James A. Robinson

sources.title: The Colonial Origins of Comparative Development: An Empirical Investigation
sources.author: Acemoglu, Johnson and Robinson

sources.title: The Colonial Origins of Comparative Development: An Empirical Investigation: Comment
sources.author: David Albouy

poli.theory.power.power-you-never-see.title: The power you can measure is the weakest kind
poli.theory.power.power-you-never-see.hook: The strongest kind of power leaves no trace: nobody fought, because nobody thought of fighting.
poli.theory.power.power-you-never-see.author: author-humanities-1
poli.theory.power.power-you-never-see.body:
Robert Dahl gave political science a clean definition in 1957: A has power over B to the extent that A can get B to do something B would otherwise not do. It is testable. Find a decision, find who wanted what, see who won. Dahl studied New Haven this way and concluded that no single elite ran the city.

Bachrach and Baratz replied in 1962 that he had looked only where the light was. There is a second face: deciding what gets decided. A committee that never puts a question on the agenda never loses a vote about it. The conflict is invisible because it is pre-emptied.

Steven Lukes added a third in 1974, the uncomfortable one. Power also shapes what people want. If a group never forms the grievance — accepts the arrangement as natural, or as its own fault — no conflict is observed at all. Lukes's test: compare what people want with what they would want under relative autonomy.

The problem, which Lukes concedes, is that the third face is nearly impossible to measure. The most consequential kind of power is precisely the kind that leaves no data behind.

recall.question: On Lukes's account, why is the third face of power so hard to study empirically?

options.text: Because elites conceal their decisions
options.why: concealed decisions are still decisions, and belong to Dahl's first face.

options.text: Because it works by shaping what people want
options.why: so there is no observable conflict to point at, only an absence.

options.text: Because it only operates in undemocratic states
options.why: Lukes's examples are mostly drawn from liberal democracies.

sources.title: Two Faces of Power
sources.author: Peter Bachrach and Morton S. Baratz
